She's pregnant, and he figures his part starts when labor does.

A lot of us think that. When I asked moms for the book what they wished someone had told their husbands, most of them wrote about the months before labor instead.

Ask her this week, "What will you need from me that you might not be able to say?" and write down what she tells you, so he can act on it when she can't explain.

Save this for the third trimester, and send it to the husband who thinks his part starts at labor.

One mom told me that near the end she was so tired she could barely talk, so the talking has to happen before labor starts.

Write her birth rules on one page this week, so he can keep them for her without stopping to ask.

Usually that's nerves. He doesn't know where to start, so he doesn't.

Pick one of these talks a week and write both your answers down, so you can come back to them when labor gets loud.

Send this to him with the slide you want to start on.

He says he's fine with the home birth, and she can tell he isn't.

A lot of dads carry some fear quietly. It doesn't make him a bad partner. Usually it means nobody has asked him yet.

Give him one private page to write the honest answer, so he can bring one line of it to you when he's ready.

Send this to the husband who goes quiet when the birth comes up.

The midwife asks if he has any questions, and he shrugs.

Lauralee, a mom of five, said the same about her own early appointments: "I had no idea what to ask." It's hard to come up with questions on the spot.

Write four questions down before the next prenatal visit, so he can ask them himself and write down what she says.

Save this for the next appointment, and send it to him the night before.
